historical_timeline.summary: Graduates from Simmons College; hired by the Boston Herald American.
Becomes moderator of Washington Week in Review and a NewsHour senior correspondent.
Moderates the vice-presidential debate and asks about AIDS among Black women.
Named co-anchor of the PBS NewsHour.
Announces a leave of a few weeks for health reasons; returns by the start of June.
Dies at a hospice in Washington, D.C., at 61; her family gives the cause as endometrial cancer, and friends describe a diagnosis at the turn of the year and treatment kept private.

claims.statement: Gwendolyn Ifill was born in Queens, New York, on September 29, 1955, the fifth of six children. Her father, a Panamanian immigrant, became a pastor in the African Methodist Episcopal Church; her mother was from Barbados. The family moved around the Northeast for her father's work and for a time lived in federally subsidized housing.

source_links.locator: Gwendolyn Ifill was born in Queens, on Sept. 29, 1955
born in New York City in 1955; both parents immigrants; federally subsidized housing
roster birth year 1955

claims.statement: She graduated from Simmons College in Boston in 1977. As a college intern at the Boston Herald American she found a racist note left for her; the paper's editors hired her after she graduated. She went on to report for the Baltimore Evening Sun, The Washington Post, The New York Times and NBC News.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern social history: a journalist who met racism early in her career and built one of the most respected careers in American news.

source_links.locator: internship at The Boston Herald; hired after her 1977 graduation

claims.statement: In 1999 she became moderator of PBS's Washington Week in Review, the first African American woman to host a major national political talk show, and a senior correspondent for the NewsHour. In 2013 she and Judy Woodruff were named co-anchors of the PBS NewsHour, the first women to jointly lead a national nightly news broadcast.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her work as an anchor and moderator anchors the modern social history.

claims.statement: She moderated the vice-presidential debates of 2004 and 2008. In the 2004 debate she asked the candidates about AIDS in the United States, citing the much higher death rate among Black women aged 25 to 44. She wrote The Breakthrough: Politics and Race in the Age of Obama (2009).
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her question in the 2004 debate drew national attention to a health disparity affecting Black women; the modern episode teaches another one.

source_links.locator: black women between the ages of 25 and 44 are 13 times more likely to die of the disease
best-selling author of The Breakthrough

claims.statement: On April 7, 2016, she told viewers she would be off the air for a few weeks; PBS described the reason as health issues it did not specify, and in May said she was doing well and expected to return around Memorial Day. She was back on the air by the start of June, when she interviewed President Obama.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The first public sign of her illness, three months after the modern index visit. The illness itself was not named in public until her death.

source_links.locator: told viewers on April 7 she would be off for the next few weeks; undisclosed health issue; return around Memorial Day

claims.statement: She kept her illness private. After her death a close friend said she had been diagnosed with cancer at the end of 2015 or early in 2016, had told family and friends, and that the April leave was due to complications of treatment; another friend described her keeping up her work through chemotherapy. PBS said she died after several months of cancer treatment.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern episode. These are friends' accounts and an official statement given after her death; the stage, histology and treatment of her cancer were never made public.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluate postmenopausal bleeding at once, as any bleeding after menopause requires, in a 60-year-old Black woman, whose risk of dying of endometrial cancer is about twice that of White women because of later diagnosis, more aggressive non-endometrioid and p53-abnormal tumors, and delays in evaluating bleeding: transvaginal ultrasound together with endometrial sampling at the first evaluation (the ACOG update that no longer relies on a thin endometrium alone); histology with the molecular classification (POLE, mismatch repair, p53) that the FIGO 2023 staging uses; CT staging; gynecologic oncology care with minimally invasive hysterectomy and sentinel lymph node mapping; treatment chosen by stage and molecular class, here dostarlimab with carboplatin and paclitaxel for mismatch repair deficient stage IIIC2 disease, with immune-related adverse event monitoring; universal Lynch syndrome tumor screening with MLH1 promoter methylation testing and genetic counseling; and survivorship care, on the NCCN uterine neoplasms guideline, the ACOG postmenopausal bleeding guidance, the SGO surveillance statement and the CMID endometrial cancer monograph.

visit_schedule.purpose: Three weeks of postmenopausal bleeding in a woman of 60: examination, office endometrial biopsy, transvaginal ultrasound, and gynecologic oncology review booked
Biopsy result: endometrial cancer; staging CT, gynecologic oncology consultation, Lynch syndrome tumor screening, and preparation for surgery
Review three weeks after surgical staging: final pathology and molecular class, genetic counseling, and the first cycle of dostarlimab with carboplatin and paclitaxel
Midpoint of combination treatment: blood counts, immune-related adverse event checks, neuropathy, and mood
End of combination treatment: response CT, immune-related hypothyroidism, the first maintenance dostarlimab dose, and the survivorship plan

hpi.narrative: Ms. Ifill returns two weeks after her first visit. The transvaginal ultrasound two days after that visit showed a 16 mm heterogeneous endometrium with internal blood flow and two small fibroids. The endometrial biopsy taken at the first visit, telephoned to her four days later, shows endometrioid adenocarcinoma, FIGO grade 2, with loss of MLH1 and PMS2 staining and a wild-type p53 pattern. CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis the next week showed an enlarged right external iliac lymph node and an enlarged left para-aortic node, with no disease in the liver, lungs, bones or peritoneum. Dr. Delacroix of gynecologic oncology saw her this morning. The bleeding has lessened to occasional spotting. She has no pain, bowel or bladder change, leg swelling or weight loss. She says she is shaken but glad the answer came quickly, and wants to keep working through treatment if she can. She has had no thoughts of self-harm.

assessment.display: Endometrioid adenocarcinoma of the endometrium, FIGO grade 2, mismatch repair deficient
assessment.assessment: The biopsy shows a low-grade endometrioid cancer that has lost MLH1 and PMS2, with a wild-type p53 pattern. The enlarged right pelvic and left para-aortic nodes on CT suggest stage IIIC disease; the final FIGO 2023 stage comes from surgery. The molecular class needs POLE sequencing on the surgical specimen as well: a POLE-mutated tumor carries an excellent outlook, a p53-abnormal one a poor outlook, and a mismatch repair deficient tumor responds strongly to immunotherapy. She is fit, and the disease on CT can be removed with a minimally invasive operation: total hysterectomy with removal of both tubes and ovaries, washings, sentinel lymph node mapping with indocyanine green, and removal of the enlarged pelvic and para-aortic nodes. If nodal disease is confirmed, I recommend dostarlimab with carboplatin and paclitaxel every three weeks for six cycles, then dostarlimab alone every six weeks for up to three years: for mismatch repair deficient advanced endometrial cancer this combination sharply lowers the risk of progression compared with chemotherapy alone. Radiation would be reserved for nodal disease left after treatment. The loss of MLH1 is the universal Lynch syndrome tumor screen; in most women of her age it comes from MLH1 promoter methylation in the tumor, which is acquired, not inherited. If methylation is found, germline testing is not needed; if it is not, she should have germline testing after counseling, and if a variant is found, her blood relatives should be offered cascade testing through a letter she can share
